source_spans.locator: Nature Neuroscience 14(11), published p.1475, Abstract: beliefs are updated more after information that is better than expected than after information that is worse than expected

Nature Neuroscience 14(11), published pp.1475-1476, task/Figure 1: participants estimate personal likelihood of adverse events, receive the average probability for a similar person, and later estimate the same events again

Nature Neuroscience 14(11), published p.1476, Behaviour/Figure 2: absolute update is greater for desirable than undesirable information, and estimation error predicts update more strongly for desirable than undesirable information

Nature Neuroscience 14(11), Methods, Main behavioural analysis: estimation error is the absolute difference between first estimate and presented probability; trials are separately classified as desirable or undesirable according to whether the initial estimate is above or below the presented probability; update is first estimate minus second estimate

conditions: participants estimate their personal likelihood of adverse future events, receive population-rate information for the same events, and later re-estimate their personal likelihoods
population: 19 healthy right-handed young adults with usable behavioural data in the main study
task: estimate-information-reestimate procedure over adverse future events
temporal_scope: the first personal estimate precedes presentation of population-rate information, which precedes the second personal estimate
